lead: A kidney stone is a hard mineral mass, often 5–10 mm across, that forms in the kidney and blocks the flow of urine. Lithotripsy breaks it into small pieces with focused shock waves, and the pieces leave the body in the urine. No cut, no open surgery. The common form is extracorporeal shock-wave lithotripsy (ESWL); extracorporeal means outside the body. It is the first treatment offered for most kidney and upper-ureter stones. Harder or deeper stones are broken from inside with a laser or an ultrasonic probe.
prereq: You need only the school physics of waves and focusing: a wave carries energy, and a curved surface can bring it to a point.

sections.h3: How a shock wave breaks a stone

blocks.text: A shock wave is a single pressure pulse, not a continuous sound. Its pressure rises to a peak in a few nanoseconds, falls, swings below zero briefly, then settles. In water the peak is tens of megapascals — hundreds of times atmospheric pressure. It carries energy, not electric charge.

Two effects break the stone. The stone is stiffer and denser than the water and tissue around it: an acoustic impedance mismatch. And the compressive pulse passes into the stone, reaches the far face, and reflects back as a tensile (pulling) wave. Brittle mineral is weak in tension, so cracks open at the back face.

Cavitation helps. The negative part of the wave pulls dissolved gas into tiny bubbles; they collapse violently and hammer the surface. The aim is fragments of 1–2 mm, which travel down the ureter with the urine; pieces of 4–5 mm or more can lodge in the ureter and block it.

sections.h3: Generating and focusing the shock wave

blocks.text: The classic source is electrohydraulic. A spark gap sits under water at the first focus F<sub>1</sub> of an ellipsoid reflector. A capacitor of about 80 nF charged to 15–25 kV discharges across the gap, the water flashes into plasma, a bubble grows and collapses, and an acoustic pulse spreads in all directions.

On an ellipsoid, the distance from focus F<sub>1</sub> to any point on the surface plus the distance from that point to focus F<sub>2</sub> is constant. Every ray leaving F<sub>1</sub> therefore travels the same path length to reach F<sub>2</sub>, so all rays arrive together and add in phase. The stone is placed at F<sub>2</sub>, where the pressure is many times the pressure near the spark.

blocks.where: P is any point on the ellipsoidal reflector; F<sub>1</sub> is the spark-gap focus; F<sub>2</sub> is the focus where the stone sits; 2a is the constant path length, in metres.

blocks.text: An electromagnetic source fires a pulse of current through a flat coil behind a metal membrane. The membrane is driven away from the coil and launches an acoustic pressure pulse into the water, and a lens or a cylindrical reflector focuses it. No electrodes wear out, so every firing of thousands is the same. A piezoelectric source mounts several hundred ceramic crystals on a spherical bowl and fires them together; the bowl curvature is the focus. The wide bowl spreads the energy over a large area of skin, so the skin and its nerves receive little and the treatment hurts less; the energy becomes intense only in the small focal zone, which must therefore be aimed precisely.

Coupling matters more than any other detail. Air reflects almost all acoustic energy, so the path from source to skin must be water or gel. Old machines used a water bath the patient sat in; modern ones use a water-filled cushion or a gel pad pressed to the flank. A trapped air bubble blocks the wave and burns the skin.

sections.h3: One session, and breaking the stone from inside

items: Locate the stone by X-ray or ultrasound and bring it onto the shock-wave axis.
Give analgesia or sedation; the patient lies on the table over the water cushion.
Couple with gel and start at low energy, raising it in steps.
Fire 2000–3000 shocks at 60–120 shocks per minute, checking position on the image.
Stop when the fragments are small enough to pass.
Advise plenty of water; fragments leave over days to weeks.

blocks.text: Rate matters. Firing quickly leaves no time for the cavitation bubbles of one shock to dissolve, so the next shock hits a bubble cloud that scatters it. Slower firing, 60 to 120 shocks per minute, gives better fragmentation and less tissue bruising, even though the session runs longer.

ESWL fails on very hard stones such as cystine, on stones above about 2 cm where the fragment load is too heavy, in obese patients where the skin-to-stone distance is long, and on stones low in the ureter where pelvic bone blocks the path. A ureteric stent, a thin plastic tube left in the ureter, keeps urine flowing so a column of fragments cannot block the kidney.

Intracorporeal lithotripsy breaks the stone from inside the body. A ureteroscope passes up the urethra and bladder to the stone. A holmium:YAG laser sends 2.1 µm light pulses down a thin silica fibre and drills the stone; an ultrasonic probe vibrates at about 20–25 kHz, breaks the stone and can suck the dust out through a hollow core. Laser suits hard stones, ultrasonic suits large soft ones.

examples.question: An electrohydraulic lithotripter charges an 80 nF capacitor to 20 kV and discharges it across the spark gap. One session delivers 2500 shocks. Find the electrical energy per shock and the total energy delivered in the session.
steps: Capacitor energy E = ½CV², with C = 80 nF = 80 × 10⁻⁹ F and V = 20 kV = 20 × 10³ V.
E = 0.5 × 80 × 10⁻⁹ F × 4 × 10⁸ V² = 16 J per shock.
Only a small part of each 16 J reaches the stone as acoustic energy; most is lost in the spark, the water path and the reflector.
examples.answer: 16 J per shock, and 40 kJ (40 000 J) for the whole session.

examples.question: An ellipsoidal reflector has a semi-major axis a = 150 mm and a semi-minor axis b = 90 mm. Find the distance from the centre to each focus, the distance between the spark at F₁ and the stone at F₂, the path length of every reflected ray, and the time a reflected pulse takes to reach the stone through water at 1500 m/s.
steps: Distance F₁F₂ = 2c = 240 mm, so the stone sits 240 mm from the spark.
Every reflected path PF₁ + PF₂ = 2a = 300 mm, whatever point P of the reflector the ray strikes.
Travel time = 0.300 m ÷ 1500 m/s = 2.0 × 10⁻⁴ s = 0.2 ms for every reflected ray, so they all arrive together.
The direct, unreflected wave covers only 240 mm and arrives in 0.16 ms, 0.04 ms earlier, but it is weak because it is not focused.
examples.answer: c = 120 mm, F₁F₂ = 240 mm, every reflected path is 300 mm and every reflected ray arrives after 0.2 ms.

traps: The word shock misleads. This is an acoustic pressure pulse; no current flows through the patient. The 20 kV stays inside the water bath or the coil circuit.

Label the foci correctly. F₁ is the near focus, inside the reflector, where the spark fires; F₂ is the far focus, outside the reflector at a fixed distance, where the stone is placed. The table is moved until the stone sits at F₂.
In ½CV² put C in farads and V in volts. Substituting 20 for 20 kV makes the energy a million times too small.
ESWL is not for every stone: stones above about 2 cm, cystine stones and stones low in the ureter usually need another method.
A ureteric stent does not treat the stone; it only keeps urine flowing while the fragments pass.

quiz.q: Define lithotripsy. What does extracorporeal mean in ESWL?
quiz.a: Lithotripsy is the breaking of a stone into fragments small enough to pass in urine. Extracorporeal means the energy source is outside the body; the wave enters through the skin.

quiz.q: Why is the reflector an ellipsoid? Name the focus used for the spark and the focus used for the stone.
quiz.a: For an ellipsoid, PF₁ + PF₂ is constant, so every ray from F₁ reflects to F₂ over the same path length and all rays arrive in phase. Spark gap at F₁, stone at F₂.

quiz.q: A 0.1 µF capacitor is charged to 18 kV and fired 3000 times in a session. Find the energy per shock and the session total.
Why is a gel pad or water cushion used between the shock source and the skin?
quiz.a: Air reflects almost all acoustic energy, so the wave would be blocked and the skin would burn at the entry point. Water and gel have impedance close to tissue, so the wave crosses with little loss.

quiz.q: Why do lithotripters fire at 60–120 shocks per minute instead of as fast as the capacitor allows?
quiz.a: Cavitation bubbles from one shock need time to dissolve. A shock arriving too soon hits the bubble cloud, which scatters and absorbs energy, so fragmentation falls and tissue injury rises. The slower rate gives more fragmentation per shock.

quiz.q: A patient has a 3 cm stone and a long skin-to-stone distance. Why may ESWL fail, and what is the alternative?
quiz.a: Above about 2 cm the fragment load is too heavy to pass and may block the ureter, and a long skin-to-stone distance may keep the stone outside the focal zone where energy density is high. Alternative: percutaneous nephrolithotomy, in which a tract is made through the flank into the kidney and the stone is broken with an ultrasonic probe or laser and removed, or laser lithotripsy through a ureteroscope; a stent keeps urine flowing afterwards.

beyond: Not for the exam. Electrohydraulic spark gaps are being replaced by electromagnetic and piezoelectric sources with solid-state switching, because the shock waveform then stays the same over a long service life. Burst-wave and histotripsy research uses trains of low-amplitude focused ultrasound to erode or liquefy tissue without any cut. Real-time ultrasound tracking that fires a shock only when the stone sits exactly at F₂ is an active engineering problem. Search for 'shock-wave lithotripsy focal zone', 'histotripsy' and 'holmium laser lithotripsy fibre'.
